tldr: Netflix published production lessons on LLM inference at scale using Triton and vLLM—practical patterns for serving multiple model sizes and hardware configurations.
Model Context Protocol (MCP) major update removes significant machinery; servers built on earlier versions will need updates.
Enterprise AI infrastructure vendors (Vultr, TensorWave, Dell) are emphasizing reliability, cost-per-performance, and operational simplicity over raw GPU specs as the market matures.

top.title: Netflix details in-house LLM serving platform with Triton and vLLM
top.summary: Netflix published production architecture for LLM inference, detailing how it uses Triton and vLLM to handle multiple model sizes and heterogeneous hardware. The writeup covers challenges in supporting rapidly evolving inference engines and different hardware requirements at scale.
top.why: If you're building a multi-model inference platform on Azure, this is a real-world pattern for the serving layer—shows what operational complexity to budget for and how to abstract over inference engine churn.

top.title: Model Context Protocol major update removes established server machinery
top.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is releasing a major update that removes significant foundational machinery that many existing servers were built around. Lead maintainers froze the release candidate.
top.why: If you have MCP servers in production or planned, this is a breaking change—you will need to evaluate and likely rewrite parts of your integration. Check the release notes before committing to MCP in any new architecture.

also.title: OpenCode static security verifier blocks unsafe AI tool calls before execution
also.summary: TypeScript plugin for OpenCode that intercepts agent tool calls (bash, read, edit, write) and verifies them against a security model before execution.

also.summary: New specification draft for making AI agent decisions deterministic and reproducible, addressing auditability and compliance concerns.
